claim: Human perception is invariably accompanied by a graded feeling of confidence that guides metacognitive awareness and decision-making.
source: Human perception is invariably accompanied by a graded feeling of confidence that guides metacognitive awareness and decision-making.
evidence: This is a general statement about human cognition that draws from established scientific understanding in the field of metacognition.

claim: Confidence is often assumed to arise solely from the feed-forward encoding of the strength or precision of sensory inputs.
source: It is often assumed that this arises solely from the feed-forward encoding of the strength or precision of sensory inputs.
evidence: This statement references a common assumption in the field, representing established theoretical perspectives.

claim: Interoceptive inference models suggest that confidence reflects a weighted integration of sensory precision and expectations about internal states, such as arousal.
source: In contrast, interoceptive inference models suggest that confidence reflects a weighted integration of sensory precision and expectations about internal states, such as arousal.
evidence: This statement describes a theoretical model from the literature on interoceptive inference.

claim: Unseen disgust-cues induced unexpected, unconscious arousal just before participants discriminated motion signals of variable precision.
source: Here we test this hypothesis using a novel psychophysical paradigm, in which unseen disgust-cues induced unexpected, unconscious arousal just before participants discriminated motion signals of variable precision.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation used in the study, which is supported by the experimental design and methods.

claim: Arousing disgust cues modulated the encoding of sensory noise across measures of perceptual bias, uncertainty, and physiological arousal.
source: Across measures of perceptual bias, uncertainty, and physiological arousal we found that arousing disgust cues modulated the encoding of sensory noise.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data across multiple measures.

claim: The degree to which trial-by-trial pupil fluctuations encoded the nonlinear interaction between arousal and sensory noise correlated with trial level confidence.
source: Furthermore, the degree to which trial-by-trial pupil fluctuations encoded this nonlinear interaction correlated with trial level confidence.
evidence: This is a finding from the pupillometry analysis showing correlation between physiological measures and confidence.

claim: Unexpected arousal regulates perceptual precision.
source: Our results suggest that unexpected arousal regulates perceptual precision, such that subjective confidence reflects the integration of both external sensory and internal, embodied states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Subjective confidence reflects the integration of both external sensory and internal, embodied states.
source: Our results suggest that unexpected arousal regulates perceptual precision, such that subjective confidence reflects the integration of both external sensory and internal, embodied states.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental results showing interactions between arousal and sensory processing.

claim: Confidence is thought to depend upon the quality or strength of sensory evidence.
source: Although confidence is thought to depend upon the quality or strength of sensory evidence, convergent computational theory and experimental data highlight the role of interoceptive inferences in guiding exteroceptive awareness.
evidence: This represents a common theoretical position in the field of metacognition research.

claim: Convergent computational theory and experimental data highlight the role of interoceptive inferences in guiding exteroceptive awareness.
source: Although confidence is thought to depend upon the quality or strength of sensory evidence, convergent computational theory and experimental data highlight the role of interoceptive inferences in guiding exteroceptive awareness.
evidence: This statement references existing theoretical and empirical work in the literature.

claim: Confidence may be a metacognitive integration of both internal and external sources of uncertainty.
source: In this sense, confidence may be a metacognitive integration of both internal and external sources of uncertainty.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposition that the study aims to test.

claim: In signal detection theory, sensory samples whose average intensity fall beyond a confidence criterion are ascribed a higher certainty.
source: For example, in signal detection theory, sensory samples whose average intensity fall beyond a confidence criterion are ascribed a higher certainty (Galvin et al., 2003; Lau and Rosenthal, 2011; Maniscalco and Lau, 2012).
evidence: This describes a computational model from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Ballistic accumulation models suggest that confidence relates to the speed of evidence accumulation relative to decision threshold.
source: Similarly, ballistic accumulation models suggest that confidence relates to the speed of evidence accumulation relative to decision threshold (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Kiani et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a computational model from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Magnetic stimulation of the motor cortex specifically disrupts confidence but not accuracy for perceptual choice.
source: However, emerging evidence suggests that confidence can be influenced independently of choice accuracy; for example magnetic stimulation of the motor cortex specifically disrupts confidence but not accuracy for perceptual choice (Fleming et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study demonstrating dissociation between confidence and accuracy.

claim: Increased sensory noise reduces confidence even when difficulty is equated.
source: Similarly, increased sensory noise reduces confidence even when difficulty is equated (Spence et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study showing the effect of sensory noise on confidence.

claim: Bodily arousal regulates affective salience and perceptual variability.
source: A potential physiological mediator of these effects is bodily arousal, which regulates affective salience and perceptual variability (Critchley et al., 2001; Murphy et al., 2014b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research on arousal.

claim: Sudden increases in arousal trigger a reciprocal cascade of central, autonomic, and peripheral responses in the brain, heart, and pupil.
source: Sudden increases in arousal trigger a reciprocal cascade of central, autonomic, and peripheral responses in the brain, heart, and pupil.
evidence: This describes established physiological responses to arousal, representing general knowledge in the field.

claim: Centrally, arousal is mediated by a reciprocal noradrenergic network with projections throughout the prefrontal, sensory, and limbic cortices.
source: Centrally, arousal is mediated by a reciprocal noradrenergic network with projections throughout the prefrontal, sensory, and limbic cortices (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Murphy et al., 2014a).
evidence: This describes the neurobiological basis of arousal, supported by citations.

claim: The noradrenergic network is important for integrating perceptual and interoceptive signals.
source: This network of areas is also important for integrating perceptual and interoceptive signals (Singer et al., 2009; Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Salomon et al., 2016), error-awareness (Fiehler et al., 2004; Klein et al., 2013), and expected confidence or volatility (Iglesias et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The noradrenergic network is important for error-awareness.
source: This network of areas is also important for integrating perceptual and interoceptive signals (Singer et al., 2009; Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Salomon et al., 2016), error-awareness (Fiehler et al., 2004; Klein et al., 2013), and expected confidence or volatility (Iglesias et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The noradrenergic network is important for expected confidence or volatility.
source: This network of areas is also important for integrating perceptual and interoceptive signals (Singer et al., 2009; Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Salomon et al., 2016), error-awareness (Fiehler et al., 2004; Klein et al., 2013), and expected confidence or volatility (Iglesias et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In predictive coding, confidence reflects the precision (or inverse variance) of a higher-order belief about both internal states and external sensations.
source: In contrast, predictive coding emphasizes interoceptive inference, in which confidence reflects the precision (or inverse variance) of a higher-order belief about both internal states and external sensations (Friston and Kiebel, 2009; Clark, 2015).
evidence: This describes a theoretical framework from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Neurobiologically, precision is encoded by the gain of local pyramidal cells.
source: Neurobiologically, precision is encoded by the gain of local pyramidal cells (Bastos et al., 2012), which is regulated across the cortical hierarchy by neuromodulators such as dopamine and noradrenaline (Feldman and Friston, 2010; Friston et al., 2012; Moran et al., 2013; Kanai et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a neurobiological mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Precision is regulated across the cortical hierarchy by neuromodulators such as dopamine and noradrenaline.
source: Neurobiologically, precision is encoded by the gain of local pyramidal cells (Bastos et al., 2012), which is regulated across the cortical hierarchy by neuromodulators such as dopamine and noradrenaline (Feldman and Friston, 2010; Friston et al., 2012; Moran et al., 2013; Kanai et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a neurobiological mechanism supported by citations.

claim: The global regulation of precision by neuromodulatory gain control entails that unexpected changes in internal states should influence the estimation of confidence for other, exteroceptive channels.
source: The global regulation of precision by neuromodulatory gain control entails that unexpected changes in internal states should influence the estimation of confidence for other, exteroceptive channels.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the predictive coding framework.

claim: Predictive coding hypothesizes that the weight given to sensory noise depends upon expected interoceptive states, such as arousal and cardiac acceleration.
source: Predictive coding thus hypothesizes that the weight given to sensory noise depends upon expected interoceptive states, such as arousal and cardiac acceleration (Gu et al., 2013; Seth, 2013; Barrett and Simmons, 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical hypothesis from the predictive coding framework, supported by citations.

claim: An unexpected increase in arousal should reduce the influence of sensory noise on confidence.
source: On this basis, we reasoned that an unexpected increase in arousal should reduce the influence of sensory noise on confidence.
evidence: This is a hypothesis derived from the theoretical framework that the study aims to test.

claim: Performance was equated across conditions such that changes in subjective uncertainty could be attributed to a precision-weighting mechanism, independently from any effect on choice accuracy.
source: Crucially, performance was equated across conditions such that changes in subjective uncertainty could be attributed to a precision-weighting mechanism, independently from any effect on choice accuracy.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claim: 29 participants performed the motion discrimination task.
source: To test these hypotheses, 29 participants performed the motion discrimination task illustrated in Figure 1.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study sample size.

claim: On every trial a global motion stimulus was preceded by a masked disgust or neutral cue.
source: On every trial a global motion stimulus was preceded by a masked disgust or neutral cue.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants discriminated the average direction of a cloud of moving dots and rated their confidence in this decision.
source: Participants then discriminated the average direction of a cloud of moving dots and rated their confidence in this decision.
evidence: This describes the task participants performed.

claim: Disgusted faces signal salient interoceptive and affective challenge.
source: We used disgusted faces as arousal cues as they signal salient interoceptive and affective challenge (Chapman and Anderson, 2012), and elicit increased arousal and physiological responses, including heart rate acceleration and facial mimicry, even when presented without awareness (Vrana, 1993; Phillips et al., 1997; Dimberg et al., 2000; Chapman and Anderson, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Disgusted faces elicit increased arousal and physiological responses, including heart rate acceleration and facial mimicry, even when presented without awareness.
source: We used disgusted faces as arousal cues as they signal salient interoceptive and affective challenge (Chapman and Anderson, 2012), and elicit increased arousal and physiological responses, including heart rate acceleration and facial mimicry, even when presented without awareness (Vrana, 1993; Phillips et al., 1997; Dimberg et al., 2000; Chapman and Anderson, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: All faces were masked from awareness, allowing us to discount any role of conscious demand characteristic in our cue-related effects.
source: Furthermore, all faces were masked from awareness, allowing us to discount any role of conscious demand characteristic in our cue-related effects.
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the study design.

claim: Staircases were stable across trials and between conditions.
source: In a series of control analyses, we confirmed that (1) staircases were stable across trials and between conditions, (2) staircases successfully controlled for potential cue-induced differences in detection difficulty, and (3) the masking procedure successfully prevented the detection of cue valence.
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses of the experimental data.

claim: Staircases successfully controlled for potential cue-induced differences in detection difficulty.
source: In a series of control analyses, we confirmed that (1) staircases were stable across trials and between conditions, (2) staircases successfully controlled for potential cue-induced differences in detection difficulty, and (3) the masking procedure successfully prevented the detection of cue valence.
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses of the experimental data.

claim: The masking procedure successfully prevented the detection of cue valence.
source: In a series of control analyses, we confirmed that (1) staircases were stable across trials and between conditions, (2) staircases successfully controlled for potential cue-induced differences in detection difficulty, and (3) the masking procedure successfully prevented the detection of cue valence.
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses of the experimental data.

claim: Adaptive staircases successfully held performance stable across blocks.
source: Analysis of detection accuracy across blocks showed that our adaptive staircases successfully held performance stable across blocks; (F(1,24), all conditions Ps >0.12, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Cues exerted no influence on motion discrimination sensitivity (d-prime), reaction times, or motion thresholds.
source: Further, cues exerted no influence on motion discrimination sensitivity (d-prime, d'), reaction times, or motion thresholds (Figure 1B, i-ii, all ps > 0.1), demonstrating that cues did not distract participants from the upcoming motion signal or otherwise alter stimulus sensitivity or detection performance.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis showing null effects, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Cues did not distract participants from the upcoming motion signal or otherwise alter stimulus sensitivity or detection performance.
source: Further, cues exerted no influence on motion discrimination sensitivity (d-prime, d'), reaction times, or motion thresholds (Figure 1B, i-ii, all ps > 0.1), demonstrating that cues did not distract participants from the upcoming motion signal or otherwise alter stimulus sensitivity or detection performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the null effects on performance measures.

claim: Analysis of d-prime for the forced-choice valence detection task showed that cues were not seen by participants.
source: Analysis of d-prime for our forced-choice valence detection task at the end of the experiment showed that cues were not seen by participants (all 95% CIs span zero, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the masking efficacy test, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Increased sensory noise (motion variance) rendered motion discrimination more difficult, slowing reaction times.
source: Replicating previous results (de Gardelle and Summerfield, 2011; Spence et al., 2016), increased sensory noise (motion variance) rendered motion discrimination more difficult, slowing reaction times (median RT, main effect Variance, F(1,24) = 4.76, p=0.039, partial η2 = 0.17,) and decreasing sensitivity (d', main effect Variance, F(1, 24) = 185.15, p<0.001, partial η2 = 0.89, see Figure 2B,i).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data, replicating previous studies.

claim: Increased sensory noise decreased sensitivity (d').
source: Replicating previous results (de Gardelle and Summerfield, 2011; Spence et al., 2016), increased sensory noise (motion variance) rendered motion discrimination more difficult, slowing reaction times (median RT, main effect Variance, F(1,24) = 4.76, p=0.039, partial η2 = 0.17,) and decreasing sensitivity (d', main effect Variance, F(1, 24) = 185.15, p<0.001, partial η2 = 0.89, see Figure 2B,i).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data, replicating previous studies.

claim: Participants were generally unbiased in their tendency to respond left or right across conditions.
source: We next assessed whether cues altered perceptual biases for motion, i.e. whether cues increased the influence of prior beliefs on stimulus classification. Although participants were generally unbiased in their tendency to respond left or right across conditions (choice criterion (c), grand mean F(1, 24) = 1.45, p=0.24), a variance × cue interaction was found such that c was increased on low variance disgust-cued trials, but reduced on high variance disgust-cued trials (V × P interaction, F(1, 24) = 10.46, p=0.004, partial η2 = 0.30).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of choice criterion.

claim: A variance × cue interaction was found such that choice criterion was increased on low variance disgust-cued trials, but reduced on high variance disgust-cued trials.
source: Although participants were generally unbiased in their tendency to respond left or right across conditions (choice criterion (c), grand mean F(1, 24) = 1.45, p=0.24), a variance × cue interaction was found such that c was increased on low variance disgust-cued trials, but reduced on high variance disgust-cued trials (V × P interaction, F(1, 24) = 10.46, p=0.004, partial η2 = 0.30).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis showing an interaction effect.

claim: On trials following neutral cues, choice criterion did not differ between noise levels.
source: Follow-up paired-samples t-tests on this effect revealed that on trials following neutral cues, c did not differ between noise levels (CB NH – NL; t(24) = 0.26, p=0.80), whereas disgust cues increased rightward bias for low variance trials (CB DH – DL t(24) = 3.76, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical tests.

claim: Disgust cues increased rightward bias for low variance trials.
source: Follow-up paired-samples t-tests on this effect revealed that on trials following neutral cues, c did not differ between noise levels (CB NH – NL; t(24) = 0.26, p=0.80), whereas disgust cues increased rightward bias for low variance trials (CB DH – DL t(24) = 3.76, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical tests.

claim: Unseen, arousing cues selectively increased biases for low noise (high precision) stimuli, in the absence of any differences in the speed or accuracy of motion discrimination.
source: These results demonstrate that unseen, arousing cues selectively increased biases for low noise (high precision) stimuli, in the absence of any differences in the speed or accuracy of motion discrimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of results on choice bias.

claim: An M-Ratio (m'/d') of one indicates optimal metacognitive sensitivity.
source: According to SDT, an M-Ratio (m'/d') of one indicates optimal metacognitive sensitivity (i.e., confidence ratings exhaust sensory information), with lower ratios indicating poorer metacognition.
evidence: This describes a property of the signal detection theory model used in the analysis.

claim: Arousing disgust cues counter-acted the conservative bias induced by high sensory noise.
source: Consistent with interoceptive inference, we found that arousing disgust cues counter-acted the conservative bias induced by high sensory noise (F(1, 24) = 6.19, p=0.020, partial η2 = 0.21), see Figure 2C,iv.
evidence: This is a primary finding from statistical analysis of M-Bias, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Following neutral cues, confidence reports were significantly more conservative for noisy stimuli.
source: Following neutral cues, confidence reports were significantly more conservative for noisy stimuli (MB NH – NL; t(24) = 2.25, p=0.034), reproducing the previously reported impact of stimulus noise on uncertainty (Spence et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis that replicates a previous study.

claim: Disgust cues reduced the effect of noise on confidence, decreasing uncertainty for high variance trials and increasing it for low-variance trials.
source: In contrast, disgust cues reduced this effect, decreasing uncertainty for high variance trials and increasing it for low-variance trials (MB DH – DL; t(24) = −0.197, p=0.85).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis showing the effect of disgust cues on confidence.

claim: Cues did not disrupt or alter metacognitive sensitivity.
source: Indeed, cues did not disrupt or alter metacognitive sensitivity; no significant effects were found for M-Ratio (all p>0.6).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis showing null effects on M-Ratio.

claim: Overall M-Ratio and M-Bias did not correlate significantly with one another.
source: Additionally, overall M-Ratio and M-Bias did not correlate significantly with one another (r = 0.37, p=0.07).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: Perceptual and metacognitive biases for noisy stimuli are selectively altered by arousing disgust cues, even in the absence of performance differences in perception or metacognition.
source: These results demonstrate that perceptual and metacognitive biases for noisy stimuli are selectively altered by arousing disgust cues, even in the absence of performance differences in perception or metacognition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of results on biases and performance.

claim: The grand mean pupil response function shows a canonical orientation response, peaking during confidence rating before returning to baseline in the 2–3 s jittered inter-trial interval.
source: Inspection of the grand mean response for each measure revealed a canonical orientation response locked to trial onset (i.e., the forward mask), as characterized by pupillary dilation (grand mean peak at 2110 ms post-baseline, Figure 3A) and heart rate deceleration (grand mean trough at 1900 ms post-baseline, Figure 4A) (Sokolov, 1963; Graham and Clifton, 1966).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of pupil data, with reference to Figure 3A and citations to classic studies.

claim: The grand mean cardiac response shows heart rate deceleration with a trough at 1900 ms post-baseline.
source: Inspection of the grand mean response for each measure revealed a canonical orientation response locked to trial onset (i.e., the forward mask), as characterized by pupillary dilation (grand mean peak at 2110 ms post-baseline, Figure 3A) and heart rate deceleration (grand mean trough at 1900 ms post-baseline, Figure 4A) (Sokolov, 1963; Graham and Clifton, 1966).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of cardiac data, with reference to Figure 4A and citations to classic studies.

claim: Sensory noise increased pupil dilation.
source: Consistent with its impact on discrimination difficulty, sensory noise increased pupil dilation (peak effect = 2121 ms post-baseline, duration 554–2377 ms, max β = 24.74, cluster p=0.014) (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966; Murphy et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of pupil data, consistent with cited previous research.

claim: Confidence showed a biphasic relationship with pupil dilation depending on trial time, marked by greater dilation during stimulus presentation but increased constriction during confidence rating.
source: Confidence showed a biphasic relationship with dilation depending on trial time, marked by greater dilation during stimulus presentation (peak dilation effect = 712 ms post-baseline (pb), max β = 11.35, Minimum Cluster p=0.038, duration 676–1560 ms post-baseline), but increased constriction during confidence rating (peak constriction effect = 2273 ms post-baseline, max β = −18.53, Minimum Cluster p=0.038, duration 676–1560 ms post-baseline), see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of pupil data, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Unseen disgust cues significantly increased both pupil dilation and cardiac acceleration.
source: Confirming that our manipulation successfully modulated arousal, unseen disgust cues significantly increased both pupil dilation and cardiac acceleration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 4c), with increased pupil dilation during motion choice (peak at 1596 ms post stimulus, duration 1686–2403 ms, max β = 21.85, cluster p=0.032) and greater cardiac acceleration during confidence ratings (peak effect 3200 ms, duration = 2900–3700 ms, max β = 0.31, cluster p=0.044).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of physiological data, with references to figures.

claim: Confidence was related to heart-rate acceleration throughout the trial, with greater confidence linked to a faster heart rate in the interval lasting from stimulus presentation to ratings.
source: Confidence was also related to heart-rate acceleration throughout the trial, with greater confidence linked to a faster heart rate in the interval lasting from stimulus presentation to ratings (peak effects at 500 ms and 3900 ms, durations 100–1000 ms and 1600–4100 ms, max β = 0.31, cluster Ps = 0.046 and 0.002), see Figure 4A.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of cardiac data, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Pupil responses encoded the interaction of cue and motion variance in the same time interval as the overall cue main effect, with cues reversing the dilatory effect of sensory noise.
source: Pupil responses also encoded the interaction of cue and motion variance in the same time interval as the overall cue main effect, with cues reversing the dilatory effect of sensory noise (peak effect 1467 ms post-baseline, duration 1492–2472 ms, min β = −21.67, cluster p=0.034, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of pupil data, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The cue-induced reversal of pupillary noise encoding was related to confidence in a positive three-way interaction.
source: Crucially, this effect was related to confidence in a positive three-way interaction (peak effect 1512 ms post-baseline, duration 683–2099 ms, max β = 21.22, cluster p=0.008, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that trial-by-trial fluctuations in subjective confidence tracked the cue-induced reversal of pupillary noise encoding.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of pupil data, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Trial-by-trial fluctuations in subjective confidence tracked the cue-induced reversal of pupillary noise encoding.
source: Crucially, this effect was related to confidence in a positive three-way interaction (peak effect 1512 ms post-baseline, duration 683–2099 ms, max β = 21.22, cluster p=0.008, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that trial-by-trial fluctuations in subjective confidence tracked the cue-induced reversal of pupillary noise encoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the three-way interaction finding.

claim: This finding mirrors our primary behavioural effect, indicating that the impact of disgust cue on confidence biases relates to a shift in the mapping between noise-induced uncertainty and physiological responses.
source: This finding mirrors our primary behavioural effect, indicating that the impact of disgust cue on confidence biases relates to a shift in the mapping between noise-induced uncertainty and physiological responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the pupil findings to the behavioral results.

claim: Cardiac signals were insensitive to sensory noise or noise by cue interactions.
source: In contrast, cardiac signals were insensitive to sensory noise or noise by cue interactions.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of cardiac data showing null effects.

claim: The magnitude of the cue-related cardiac main effect negatively interacted with confidence.
source: Instead, the magnitude of the cue-related cardiac main effect negatively interacted with confidence (peak effect 2800 ms post-baseline, duration 2800–3200 ms, min β = −0.30, cluster p=0.044), supporting a reversal in the mapping between heart rate acceleration and subjective uncertainty (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of cardiac data, with reference to Figure 4C,D.

claim: Experimentally induced increases in arousal disrupt the typical relationship of heart-rate acceleration and confidence.
source: This latter effect demonstrates that experimentally induced increases in arousal disrupt the typical relationship of heart-rate acceleration and confidence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cardiac interaction finding.

claim: The integration of expected internal state and the precision of sensory inputs is consistent with an interoceptive inference mechanism.
source: This integration of expected internal state and the precision of sensory inputs is consistent with an interoceptive inference mechanism (Seth, 2013; Barrett and Simmons, 2015), and strongly supports a role for decision-independent sources in guiding confidence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of theoretical frameworks, supported by citations.

claim: The results strongly support a role for decision-independent sources in guiding confidence.
source: This integration of expected internal state and the precision of sensory inputs is consistent with an interoceptive inference mechanism (Seth, 2013; Barrett and Simmons, 2015), and strongly supports a role for decision-independent sources in guiding confidence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall pattern of results.

claim: This study motivates a revised view of metacognition as incorporating beliefs about both physiological states and the precision of actual sensory inputs.
source: This study thus motivates a revised view of metacognition as incorporating beliefs about both physiological states and the precision of actual sensory inputs.
evidence: This is a theoretical implication drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Trial-by-trial confidence correlates with interoceptive arousal, as indexed by both cardiac acceleration and pupil dilation.
source: In general, we demonstrate consistent correlations of trial-by-trial confidence with interoceptive arousal, as indexed by both cardiac acceleration and pupil dilation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the physiological analyses.

claim: Pupil dilation covaried biphasically with subjective confidence, reversing from positive to negative during subjective ratings.
source: In contrast to the linear positive correlation observed for cardiac acceleration, pupil dilation covaried biphasically with subjective confidence, reversing from positive to negative during subjective ratings (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of pupil data, with reference to a figure.

claim: The biphasic pupil-confidence relationship may partially account for recent findings that distinct stimulus-related and post-decisional computations underlie the representation of confidence.
source: This result may partially account for recent findings that distinct stimulus-related and post-decisional computations underlie the representation of confidence (Lebreton et al., 2015; Rahnev et al., 2015), and corroborates the previously reported link between pupil variability and confidence for an auditory discrimination task (Lempert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the current findings to previous research, supported by citations.

claim: The biphasic pupil-confidence relationship corroborates the previously reported link between pupil variability and confidence for an auditory discrimination task.
source: This result may partially account for recent findings that distinct stimulus-related and post-decisional computations underlie the representation of confidence (Lebreton et al., 2015; Rahnev et al., 2015), and corroborates the previously reported link between pupil variability and confidence for an auditory discrimination task (Lempert et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement relates the current findings to a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: Interoceptive (cardiac) sensitivity and meta-cognition for memory have previously been related to one another.
source: Furthermore, although interoceptive (i.e., cardiac) sensitivity and meta-cognition for memory have previously been related to one another (Garfinkel et al., 2013), our study is the first to show that confidence reports for perception correlate positively with cardiac acceleration.
evidence: This statement references a previous finding from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: This study is the first to show that confidence reports for perception correlate positively with cardiac acceleration.
source: Furthermore, although interoceptive (i.e., cardiac) sensitivity and meta-cognition for memory have previously been related to one another (Garfinkel et al., 2013), our study is the first to show that confidence reports for perception correlate positively with cardiac acceleration.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: The results demonstrate a close link between perceptual confidence and interoceptive arousal, even when accounting for decision difficulty.
source: These results thus demonstrate a close link between perceptual confidence and interoceptive arousal, even when accounting for decision difficulty.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of physiological results.

claim: Disgust cues evoked task-orthogonal, unpredictable increases in both cardiac and pupillary responses.
source: Our disgust cues evoked task-orthogonal, unpredictable increases in both cardiac and pupillary responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the physiological effects of the disgust cues.

claim: Arousal prediction errors counter-acted the influence of sensory noise on confidence.
source: These 'arousal prediction errors' (APEs) counter-acted the influence of sensory noise on confidence, supporting the recent proposal that interoceptive inference weights the confidence or precision of exteroceptive sensory signals (Seth, 2013; Barrett and Simmons, 2015; Chanes and Barrett, 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results, interpreted in the context of theoretical proposals supported by citations.

claim: The impact of cues on the encoding of sensory noise in pupillary signals correlated with trial-by-trial confidence.
source: This mechanism was also evident in pupillary signals, where the impact of cues on the encoding of sensory noise correlated with trial-by-trial confidence.
evidence: This is a finding from the pupillometry analysis.

claim: Pupil dilation has previously been shown to relate to the overall gain or representational stability of the cortical hierarchy.
source: Pupil dilation has previously been shown to relate to the overall gain or representational stability of the cortical hierarchy (Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990; Eldar et al., 2013; Cheadle et al., 2014; for review, see Hauser et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement references previous research on pupil dilation, supported by citations.

claim: Pupil variability indexes the impact of unexpected arousal on perceptual precision.
source: Our results corroborate this proposal, suggesting that pupil variability indexes the impact of unexpected arousal on perceptual precision.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pupil findings in the context of previous research.

claim: While cues shifted the relative mapping of heart rate and confidence, sensory noise did not influence the heart.
source: In contrast, while cues also shifted the relative mapping of heart rate and confidence, we did not observe an influence of sensory noise on the heart.
evidence: This is a finding from the cardiac analysis showing a null effect.

claim: The cardiac effects may simply be downstream of cue-induced central nervous system arousal.
source: This may reflect either an issue of causality – our cardiac effects may simply be downstream of cue-induced central nervous system arousal – or it may reflect a more specific encoding of interoceptive but not exteroceptive certainty.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cardiac findings.

claim: The cardiac effects may reflect a more specific encoding of interoceptive but not exteroceptive certainty.
source: This may reflect either an issue of causality – our cardiac effects may simply be downstream of cue-induced central nervous system arousal – or it may reflect a more specific encoding of interoceptive but not exteroceptive certainty.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cardiac findings.

claim: Future pharmacological studies using cardiac or noradrenergic-specific blockades will be essential to further tease apart these mechanisms.
source: Future pharmacological studies using cardiac or noradrenergic-specific blockades will be essential to further tease apart these mechanisms.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The manipulation of arousal was by design independent from discrimination accuracy.
source: Because our manipulation of arousal was by design independent from discrimination accuracy, these results are difficult to accommodate within feed-forward observer models, which posit that confidence depends solely on the information determining stimulus detection (Galvin et al., 2003; Lau and Rosenthal, 2011; Maniscalco and Lau, 2012).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: The results are difficult to accommodate within feed-forward observer models, which posit that confidence depends solely on the information determining stimulus detection.
source: Because our manipulation of arousal was by design independent from discrimination accuracy, these results are difficult to accommodate within feed-forward observer models, which posit that confidence depends solely on the information determining stimulus detection (Galvin et al., 2003; Lau and Rosenthal, 2011; Maniscalco and Lau, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in relation to existing theoretical models, supported by citations.

claim: Arousal might alter the overall rate of evidence accumulation or the decision threshold.
source: For example, one possibility is that arousal alters the overall rate of evidence accumulation or the decision threshold (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation, referencing theoretical models from the literature.

claim: On an evidence accumulation model, arousal would increase confidence by offsetting the overall impact of sensory noise.
source: On this model, arousal would increase confidence by offsetting the overall impact of sensory noise.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction from an alternative theoretical model.

claim: A dynamic or two-stage model could potentially account for decision-independent reductions in confidence if arousal linearly shifts the confidence criterion.
source: Similarly, a dynamic or two-stage model could potentially account for decision-independent reductions in confidence (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010), if arousal linearly shifts the confidence criterion.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation, referencing a theoretical model from the literature.

claim: Neither evidence accumulation nor two-stage models would predict the nonlinear interaction of unexpected arousal and confidence observed in this study.
source: However, neither model would predict the nonlinear interaction of unexpected arousal and confidence observed here.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of alternative models in explaining the current findings.

claim: Disgust cues seemed to enhance a slight rightward bias for high precision stimuli.
source: Interestingly, we also observed an interaction between cue valence and sensory noise for participant response bias. Although all participants were right handed, disgust cues seemed to enhance a slight rightward bias for high precision stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of response bias.

claim: This result may point to a role for unconscious arousal in strengthening the influence of priors on perceptual inference.
source: This result may point to a role for unconscious arousal in strengthening the influence of priors on perceptual inference.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the response bias finding.

claim: The prevalence for participants to engage in the 'gambler's fallacy' is well documented.
source: Although motion directions were presented randomly across trials, the prevalence for participants to engage in the 'gambler's fallacy', in which a 'streak' of repeated outcomes leads to increased belief that this outcome is more likely, is well documented (Tversky and Kahneman, 1971, 1974).
evidence: This statement references a well-known cognitive bias from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: By boosting the precision of pre-stimulus beliefs, participants come to believe that stimuli following arousing cues will conform to their erroneous motion expectations.
source: The suggestion here is that by boosting the precision of pre-stimulus beliefs (i.e., expected precision), participants come to believe that stimuli following arousing cues will conform to their (erroneous) motion expectations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how arousal might influence perceptual biases.

claim: This interpretation is consistent with the more general role of expected precision in bottom-up and top-down attention.
source: This interpretation is consistent with the more general role of expected precision in bottom-up and top-down attention (Feldman and Friston, 2010).
evidence: This statement relates the interpretation to a theoretical framework from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Neurobiologically, expected precision (or volatility) is implemented through gain control by neuromodulation, as regulated by insular, cingulate, pulvinar and other limbic areas rich in neuromodulatory neurons.
source: Neurobiologically, expected precision (or volatility) is implemented through gain control by neuromodulation, as regulated by insular, cingulate, pulvinar and other limbic areas rich in neuromodulatory neurons (Friston et al., 2012; Moran et al., 2013; Schwartenbeck et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a neurobiological mechanism from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Active inference models suggest that the regulation of expected precision is a central mechanism underlying both bottom-up (salience) and top-down attention.
source: Active inference models suggest that the regulation of expected precision is a central mechanism underlying both bottom-up (i.e., salience) and top-down attention (Feldman and Friston, 2010; Moran et al., 2013; Kanai et al., 2015)
evidence: This describes a theoretical model from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The sudden increase in arousal elicited by cues may correspond to an inflation of expected precision, which would reduce the salience of sensory (exteroceptive) gain in perceptual inference.
source: Thus, the sudden increase in arousal elicited by cues may correspond to an inflation of expected precision, which would reduce the salience of sensory (exteroceptive) gain in perceptual inference.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: The study does not explicitly manipulate the underlying probability of receiving an arousing cue.
source: However, here we do not explicitly manipulate the underlying probability of receiving an arousing cue.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the current study design.

claim: To conclusively determine how the interaction of arousal prediction and expected precision shapes confidence, future work should explicitly manipulate the volatility of interoceptive fluctuations by altering the underlying probability of an arousal change point.
source: To conclusively determine how the interaction of arousal prediction and expected precision shapes confidence, future work should explicitly manipulate the volatility of interoceptive fluctuations by altering the underlying probability of an arousal change point (Behrens et al., 2007; Summerfield et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research, referencing relevant methodological approaches from the literature.

claim: Although the study manipulates arousal and observes correlated changes in cardiac signals and confidence, the causal link to interoception must be established in future investigations.
source: Additionally, although here we manipulate arousal and observe correlated changes in cardiac signals and confidence, the causal link to interoception must be established in future investigations, in which cardiac signals are directly manipulated independently of the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the current study and a suggestion for future research.

claim: Hierarchical psycho-physiological computational modelling could further reveal the interoceptive computations underlying perceptual confidence.
source: This approach, coupled with hierarchical psycho-physiological computational modelling (de Berker et al., 2016), could further reveal the interoceptive computations underlying perceptual confidence.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research, referencing a methodological approach from the literature.

claim: The study demonstrates a close linkage of perceptual confidence, unexpected arousal, and related interoceptive signals.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate a close linkage of perceptual confidence, unexpected arousal, and related interoceptive signals.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Across perceptual, physiological, and subjective measures the study demonstrates that the encoding of sensory noise is weighted by interoceptive arousal.
source: Across perceptual, physiological, and subjective measures we demonstrate that the encoding of sensory noise is weighted by interoceptive arousal.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: These results may have important implications for understanding medical and psychiatric disorders, in which patients exhibit chronic alterations in arousal or interoception.
source: These results may have important implications for understanding medical and psychiatric disorders, in which patients exhibit chronic alterations in arousal or interoception.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical implications of the findings.

claim: Substance abuse, psychosis, anxiety, and depression have been linked to altered heart-rate variability, physiological responses, and interoceptive sensitivity.
source: Substance abuse, psychosis, anxiety, and depression for example have been linked to altered heart-rate variability, physiological responses, and interoceptive sensitivity (Dawson et al., 1977; Hoehn-Saric and McLeod, 2000).
evidence: This statement references previous research on psychiatric disorders, supported by citations.

claim: The altered psychophysiology of patients with psychiatric disorders may cause them to perceive an unrealistically (un)-certain world.
source: Our results suggest that the altered psychophysiology of these patients may cause them to perceive an unrealistically (un)-certain world.
evidence: This is a speculative implication of the findings for understanding psychiatric disorders.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
source: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: Participants received monetary compensation (£15) for completing the experiment.
source: Participants received monetary compensation (£15) for completing the experiment.
evidence: This describes the compensation provided to participants.

claim: Informed consent was obtained from all participants.
source: Informed consent was obtained from all participants, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with approval from the UCL Research Ethics Committee.
evidence: This describes the ethical procedures followed in the study.

claim: All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with approval from the UCL Research Ethics Committee.
source: Informed consent was obtained from all participants, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with approval from the UCL Research Ethics Committee.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Participants completed 10 blocks of a psychophysical metacognition task consisting of 640 trials divided evenly between four conditions.
source: Participants completed 10 blocks of a psychophysical metacognition task consisting of 640 trials divided evenly between four conditions, with enforced breaks following each 64 trial block.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Physiological signals (ECG and pupillometry) were monitored throughout the experiment.
source: Physiological signals (ECG and pupillometry) were monitored throughout the experiment.
evidence: This describes the physiological measures collected during the study.

claim: At the conclusion of the experiment, participants completed 200 trials of a forced-choice cue-identity detection task to quantify masking efficacy.
source: At the conclusion of the experiment, participants were, (1) asked if they had noticed anything unusual about the presented faces, (2), debriefed that on half the trials there had been a hidden emotional face, and (3) completed 200 trials of a forced-choice cue-identity detection task to quantify masking efficacy.
evidence: This describes the post-task procedure to assess masking efficacy.

claim: Motion stimuli comprised a random dot stimulus moving in an approximately upward-vertical direction.
source: Motion stimuli comprised a random dot stimulus moving in an approximately upward-vertical direction.
evidence: This describes the visual stimuli used in the experiment.

claim: The stimuli were always presented at 100% coherence.
source: The stimuli were always presented at 100% coherence, that is, all dots were "signal dots" but the distribution of motion vectors was varied parametrically.
evidence: This describes a property of the motion stimuli.

claim: To control discrimination performance, the mean signal was controlled across trials using an adaptive 2 up 1down staircase which converges on 70.7% accuracy.
source: To control discrimination performance, the mean signal (the average direction of dots) was controlled across trials using an adaptive 2 up 1down staircase which converges on 70.7% accuracy (Cornsweet, 1962; Fleming and Lau, 2014).
evidence: This describes the adaptive staircase procedure used to control task difficulty, with citations to methodological references.

claim: Disgust and neutral trials were thresholded separately to allow for the possibility of the priming condition contributing to detection accuracy.
source: Disgust and neutral trials were thresholded separately to allow for the possibility of the priming condition contributing to detection accuracy (although overall they did not).
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the experimental design.

claim: Sensory noise was manipulated independently by adjusting the standard deviation of the mean direction across conditions.
source: Sensory noise was manipulated independently by adjusting the standard deviation of the mean direction across conditions.
evidence: This describes how sensory noise was manipulated in the experiment.

claim: 1000 black dots of radius 0.08 degrees visual angle were presented for 250 ms within a 15.69 DVA diameter circular array at random starting positions.
source: 1000 black dots of radius 0.08 degrees visual angle (DVA) were presented for 250 ms within a 15.69 DVA diameter circular array at random starting positions, with dots advancing 0.06 DVA per frame.
evidence: This describes the specific parameters of the motion stimulus.

claim: All dots had a randomized limited lifetime of maximum 93% (14 frames) to prevent fixation on local motion directions.
source: To prevent fixation on the local motion directions, all dots had a randomized limited lifetime of maximum 93% (14 frames).
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the motion stimulus design.

claim: Four paired male faces showing forward-directed disgust or neutral expressions were selected from the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces database.
source: For emotional face cues, four paired male faces showing forward-directed disgust or neutral expressions were selected from the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces database (KDEF; Lundqvist et al., 1998)
evidence: This describes the source of the face stimuli used in the experiment.

claim: Disgusted faces were selected based on highest mean arousal and intensity scores.
source: Disgusted faces were selected based on highest mean arousal and intensity scores (Goeleven et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for the disgust face stimuli, with a citation to the source of the ratings.

claim: A combination of forward and backwards masking was used to ensure cues were not consciously visible.
source: Following established protocols, we used a combination of forward and backwards masking to ensure cues were not consciously visible (Bachmann and Francis, 2013; Overgaard and Overgaard, 2015).
evidence: This describes the masking procedure, with citations to methodological references.

claim: Confidence was rated by moving a small triangular slider along the confidence line using the left and right arrow keys, and recorded as a 0–100 integer.
source: Confidence was rated by moving a small triangular slider along the confidence line using the left and right arrow keys, and recorded as a 0–100 integer.
evidence: This describes the method for collecting confidence ratings.

claim: To prevent response preparation the starting point of the slider on each trial was randomly jittered up to 12% to the left or right of the scale midpoint on every trial.
source: To prevent response preparation the starting point of the slider on each trial was randomly jittered up to 12% to the left or right of the scale midpoint on every trial (Fleming et al., 2012; Fleming and Lau, 2014).
evidence: This describes a methodological feature to prevent response bias, with citations to methodological references.

claim: All stimuli were presented on a grey background at mean luminance.
source: All stimuli were presented on a grey background at mean luminance.
evidence: This describes the visual presentation parameters.

claim: Face stimuli were set to grayscale and pre-processed using the SHINE toolbox in MATLAB, which uses a histogram-matching procedure to balance images both in terms of average luminance and local statistical properties.
source: Face stimuli were set to grayscale and pre-processed using the SHINE toolbox in MATLAB, which uses a histogram-matching procedure to balance images both in terms of average luminance and local statistical properties (Willenbockel et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the image processing procedure, with a citation to the toolbox reference.

claim: A minimum 6 s inter-response interval was used to allow pupil recovery.
source: To stabilize pupil signals across trials, we also adapted our stimuli timings, ITIs, and use of isoluminant dot masks on the basis of a prior dot motion pupillometry study, ensuring a minimum 6 s inter-response interval (IRI) to allow pupil recovery (Murphy et al., 2014b).
evidence: This describes a methodological feature based on previous research, with a citation.

claim: ECG signals were measured using disposable Ag/AgCl bipolar surface electrodes affixed just below the left and right clavicle and a ground electrode affixed to the nape of the neck.
source: ECG signals were measured using disposable Ag/AgCl bipolar surface electrodes (100 Foam, Covidien) affixed just below the left and right clavicle and a ground electrode affixed to the nape of the neck using medical tape and Spectra 360 salt-free electrode gel (Parker Laboratories).
evidence: This describes the ECG recording procedure.

claim: ECG signals were amplified using an Asalab System and recorded via Visor2 2.0 software at a 1024 Hz sampling rate.
source: ECG signals were amplified using an Asalab System (ANT Neuro Recording) and recorded via Visor2 2.0 software at a 1024 Hz sampling rate.
evidence: This describes the ECG recording equipment and parameters.

claim: Changes in pupil diameter were monitored using an Eyelink 1000 eye tracker recording at 1000 Hz sampling rate.
source: Changes in pupil diameter were monitored using an Eyelink 1000 eye tracker (SR research) recording at 1000 Hz sampling rate, and synchronized to the stimulus PC using the Eyelink Toolbox, for PsychToolbox (RRID:SCR_002881) (Cornelissen et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the pupillometry recording equipment and parameters, with a citation.

claim: In three participants, thresholds failed to stabilize resulting in extreme (>3 SD) median signal orientations.
source: In three participants, thresholds failed to stabilize resulting in extreme (>3 SD) median signal orientations.
evidence: This describes participant exclusions based on data quality.

claim: A fourth participant exhibited extreme confidence behaviour (> 75% of trials marked 100% confidence), resulting in four total exclusions from behavioural analyses.
source: A fourth participant exhibited extreme confidence behaviour (> 75% of trials marked 100% confidence), resulting in four total exclusions from behavioural analyses, final N = 25.
evidence: This describes participant exclusions based on data quality.

claim: The first 25% of trials were excluded from behavioural analyses to allow staircase stabilization.
source: To allow staircase stabilization, the first 25% of trials (i.e. the first two blocks) were excluded from behavioural analyses, as well as any missed trials or trials with outlier RTs (i.e. absolute z-scored RT > 3).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion criteria for behavioral analysis.

claim: Confidence ratings were binned into four quartiles to facilitate signal-theoretic modelling.
source: To facilitate signal-theoretic modelling, confidence ratings were binned into four quartiles (Maniscalco and Lau, 2012; Fleming and Lau, 2014).
evidence: This describes a data processing step for the metacognitive analysis, with citations to methodological references.

claim: The Meta-d' model quantifies an individual's introspective sensitivity and bias while controlling for the confounding impact of type-I performance.
source: By comparing the actual metacognitive sensitivity to expected (e.g. M-prime/D-prime), the Meta-d' model quantifies an individual's introspective sensitivity and bias while controlling for the confounding impact of type-I performance (see Maniscalco and Lau, 2012 for a full methodological treatment).
evidence: This describes a property of the Meta-d' model used in the analysis, with a citation.

claim: Pupil data were imported and pre-processed in MATLAB using the Fieldtrip package.
source: Pupil data were imported and pre-processed in MATLAB using the Fieldtrip package (RRID:SCR_004849, Oostenveld et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the software used for pupil data analysis, with a citation.

claim: Blinks were detected as any sample in which amplitude dropped below 600 arbitrary units dilation and were linearly interpolated.
source: Blinks were detected as any sample in which amplitude dropped below 600 arbitrary units dilation and were linearly interpolated, such that if any trial began or ended with a blink the interpolation was based on the first reliable sample.
evidence: This describes the blink detection and correction procedure for pupil data.

claim: Any trial where more than 25% of samples were marked as blinks were rejected from the analysis.
source: Any trial where more than 25% of samples were marked as blinks were rejected from the analysis.
evidence: This describes the trial exclusion criteria for pupil data.

claim: These procedures resulted in a mean rejection rate of 19.30% (SD = 9.33) of trials across participants for pupil data.
source: These procedures resulted in a mean rejection rate of 19.30% (SD = 9.33) of trials across participants.
evidence: This reports the data loss rate for pupil analysis.

claim: Pupil measures could not be obtained from two participants due to technical difficulties at recording, and one additional participant was rejected due to excessive blink artefacts, resulting in a final N = 26 for pupil analysis.
source: Pupil measures could not be obtained from two participants due to technical difficulties at recording, and one additional participant was rejected due to excessive blink artefacts, resulting in a final N = 26.
evidence: This describes participant exclusions for pupil analysis.

claim: QRS complex detection was implemented on the raw ECG data using the Pan-Tomkins algorithm.
source: QRS complex detection was implemented on the raw data after downsampling to 200 Hz with the Pan-Tomkins algorithm (Pan and Tompkins, 1985) and supplemented by manual inspection and editing.
evidence: This describes the method for detecting heartbeats in ECG data, with a citation.

claim: Artefactual ECG samples were manually marked and removed from analyses, resulting in a 6.9% (SD = 7.8) mean rejection rate.
source: Artefactual samples were then manually marked and removed from analyses, resulting in a 6.9% (SD = 7.8) mean rejection rate.
evidence: This reports the data loss rate for cardiac analysis.

claim: Instantaneous heart rate was calculated using the IBI and converted to a continuous time series by interpolating the heart rate using spline interpolation.
source: Instantaneous heart rate was calculated using the IBI and converted to a continuous time series by interpolating the heart rate (using spline interpolation), upsampling to a 10 Hz sampling rate.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating continuous heart rate from ECG data.

claim: Each trial was baseline corrected for the pre-stimulus interval before physiological timeseries analysis.
source: Following pre-processing, pupillary and ECG time series were analysed using a hierarchical general linear modelling approach. To do so, each trial was first baseline corrected for the pre-stimulus interval.
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step for physiological data analysis.

claim: A hierarchical general linear modelling approach was used to analyze pupillary and ECG time series.
source: Following pre-processing, pupillary and ECG time series were analysed using a hierarchical general linear modelling approach.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method for physiological data.

claim: A cluster-based permutation test was used to correct for multiple comparisons in the physiological timeseries analysis.
source: Using a summary statistic approach, we tested the consistency of the individual time series at the group level conducting t-tests for the positive and negative effect of each regressor, corrected for multiple comparisons using a standard cluster-based permutation test (p <0.05 cluster-extent correction, n = 500 permutations, height threshold t = 2) (Hayasaka et al., 2004; Hunt et al., 2013; Hauser et al., 2015) using custom code in MATLAB.
evidence: This describes the multiple comparisons correction method, with citations to methodological references.
